clue.text: Minor tremors, perhaps, unimpressive?

definitions.meaning: read literally, small earthquakes are tremors that are not big shakings
the idiom means mediocre, nothing special

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for something mediocre is read literally as a description of feeble earth tremors.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something mediocre or not very good, which is what unimpressive means.

clue.text: One down in a burrow?

parts.note: down means depressed, and a creature living in a burrow is a rabbit, so a gloomy rabbit

explanation.walkthrough: 'down' means unhappy, not underground; the informal idiom for a disgruntled person is read literally as a sad rabbit.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal idiom describes someone displeased or fed up, pictured as a sad rabbit.

clue.text: Approach not a dying man

indicators.note: not tells us to leave out the letter given by a

parts.note: to go near is to approach

explanation.surface: Someone is told not to approach a man who is dying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' drops A from GO NEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A goner is someone beyond help, about to die.

clue.text: Former husband I assaulted: this carries a charge, to be fair

parts.note: ex means former
bit, as of a dog, is to have assaulted with the teeth
an ion is an atom carrying an electric charge

explanation.surface: An ex-husband faces charges for assault, which seems only fair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charge' looks legal but is electrical; 'fair' is a noun, a show, not an adjective meaning just.
explanation.definitionFit: An exhibition is a public show, which is one sense of a fair, as in a trade fair.

clue.text: Tom raised hat, being sensitive

indicators.note: raised, in a down clue, means the word reads upwards

parts.note: a tom is a male cat
tile is old slang for a hat

explanation.surface: Tom lifted his hat, a considerate gesture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns CAT upward into TAC. TILE is old British slang for a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Tactile means relating to touch, so sensitive to the touch.

clue.text: A service in Nazi control

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: Rudolf Hess was a leading Nazi
RN, the Royal Navy, is one of the armed services

explanation.surface: A branch of the armed forces falls under Nazi command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal; Rudolf Hess was Hitler's deputy, which makes the Nazi a surname rather than a generic word.
explanation.definitionFit: To harness something is to bring it under control and use it.

clue.text: Thrill to be a footballer?

definitions.meaning: a buzz or rush of excitement
a footballer's basic action is to strike the ball with the foot

explanation.definitionFit: A kick can be a buzz of excitement, and kicking the ball is what a footballer does.

clue.text: Poisoner succeeded, if he's not twitching

indicators.note: twitching suggests the letters jerk about into a new order

explanation.surface: A poisoner got away with it, provided the victim stopped twitching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twitching' rearranges IF HES NOT into TONEFISH after S. The answer is a venomous fish, not a murderer.
explanation.definitionFit: The stonefish carries venomous spines, so the fish is a poisoner of the unwary.

clue.text: How one pays for cocaine addiction?

definitions.text: How one pays for cocaine addiction?

parts.words: How one pays for cocaine addiction?
parts.note: an idiom for paying too much, read literally since cocaine is taken by snorting

explanation.walkthrough: To pay over the odds is to pay by this idiom; cocaine is snorted, which brings the nose in literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means paying an excessively high price, and cocaine is literally inhaled by snorting.

clue.text: Fish smell when beheaded

indicators.note: beheading a word cuts off its first letter

parts.note: a stench is a bad smell

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a fish only smells once its head is cut off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when beheaded' removes the S from STENCH.
explanation.definitionFit: The tench is a freshwater fish of the carp family.

clue.text: Church has chortle about old shroud

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: about suggests the letters of chortle are moved around into a new order

explanation.surface: A congregation laughs at an ancient burial cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is the anagram signal, giving RECLOTH; 'has' merely links the church to what follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A cerecloth was a waxed cloth formerly used for wrapping the dead, a historic shroud.

clue.text: Might breakfast be so tough?

parts.note: eggs at breakfast can be cooked firm, and the same compound word describes a tough, unsentimental person

explanation.walkthrough: The breakfast is an egg cooked until solid; the word also means hard-bitten or unsentimental.
explanation.definitionFit: A cooked egg set firm and a tough, cynical character share this compound adjective.

clue.text: Duck seen in boozer, oddly

indicators.note: oddly suggests the found letters are arranged in a strange new order
the letters are found inside the word boozer, without its first two

explanation.surface: A duck is spotted in a pub, which is a strange sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen in' picks OZER out of bOOZER and 'oddly' rearranges it. In cricket a duck is a score of nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a duck is a batsman's score of nothing, hence nil.

clue.text: Motoring fanatic hoped later to go touring

indicators.note: touring suggests the letters travel about into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A car enthusiast hopes to go on a road trip later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go touring' rearranges the letters of HOPED LATER.
explanation.definitionFit: A petrolhead is British slang for a car enthusiast.

clue.text: Gerbil, perhaps, put in hole bearing laboratory equipment

indicators.note: put in tells us one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: a pit is a hole in the ground
a gerbil is an example of a pet
E, east, is a compass bearing

explanation.surface: Someone drops a pet gerbil into a hole along with some lab apparatus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put in' is the container signal, making PIPETT; 'bearing' is a compass point, not carrying.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipette is a slender glass tube used in laboratories to measure small volumes of liquid.

clue.text: Englishman abroad arresting crawlers, an officer

indicators.note: arresting means holding, so the first word holds the second inside it

parts.note: pom is Australian slang for an English person
lice are crawling insects

explanation.surface: An expatriate Englishman detaining some creeps turns out to be an officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arresting' is the container signal; POM is Australian slang for an English immigrant, hence 'abroad'.
explanation.definitionFit: A police officer is a policeman.

clue.text: Partners involved in deception appearing anxious

indicators.note: involved in says one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a sting is a confidence trick or deception
in bridge, East and West are partners

explanation.surface: Two people caught up in a con trick start to look worried.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved in' is the container signal. Bridge players sit as partner pairs North-South and East-West.
explanation.definitionFit: Stewing informally means fretting or worrying, so being in a stew is feeling anxious.

clue.text: Lumberjacks initially look to cut trees in shades of autumn?

indicators.note: to cut means these letters slice into the other word

parts.note: yews are evergreen trees

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of Lumberjacks

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: Lumberjacks set about felling trees amid the colours of autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' gives L, and 'to cut' puts L plus LO into YEWS.
explanation.definitionFit: Autumn leaves turn yellow, so yellows are shades seen in autumn, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Left in wild, seeking rescue

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: savage means wild or untamed

explanation.surface: Someone abandoned in the wilderness is looking to be saved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts L inside SAVAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Salvage is the rescue of property, especially a ship or its cargo, from loss.

clue.text: Range to share out

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are scattered and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone describes how a range of goods is to be divided up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges the seven letters of TO SHARE.
explanation.definitionFit: Earshot is the range within which a sound can be heard.

clue.text: 21 group of nations over the valley, getting answer

indicators.note: over in a down clue means placed above the next piece

parts.note: the EU is a union of nations
a glen is a valley, especially in Scotland

explanation.surface: A union of countries above a valley gets its answer.
explanation.walkthrough: '21' refers to the answer at 21 across: euglena is a single-celled organism with a whip-like flagellum.
explanation.definitionFit: Euglena is a single-celled organism that swims with a flagellum, so it is classed as a flagellate.

clue.text: Rare, or half rare?

indicators.note: half asks for just the first four of the eight letters of the synonym

parts.note: rare means uncommon

explanation.surface: A puzzle asks whether something is rare or only half rare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' keeps the first half of UNCOMMON. The answer is a Scots word meaning strange or remarkable.
explanation.definitionFit: Unco is Scots for unusual or remarkable, so rare in the sense of exceptional.

clue.text: Whip, having standard to raise, buttonholing Liberal

parts.note: a standard is a flag

indicators.note: buttonholing means taking hold of, so the first word grips the second inside it

parts.note: to elate is to raise the spirits

explanation.surface: A whip is used to hoist a banner while collaring a Liberal politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'buttonholing' puts L inside ELATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To flagellate is to whip or flog someone.

clue.text: Fiddle I tucked under a rug

indicators.note: tucked under means the first piece is placed below the others in this down clue

parts.note: a mat is a small rug

explanation.surface: A violin is hidden under a rug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddle' looks like a verb, but it is a violin: the Amati family of Cremona made famous ones.
explanation.definitionFit: An Amati is a violin made by the Amati family of Cremona, and fiddle is another word for violin.

clue.text: Image underlining Gable's last, great film

indicators.note: underlining in a down clue means the second piece sits beneath the first
last points to the final letter of Gable

parts.note: a pic is an image or picture

explanation.surface: A still of Clark Gable is used to promote a great film.
explanation.walkthrough: Clark Gable was a Hollywood star, which makes the film reading convincing.
explanation.definitionFit: An epic is a grand, large-scale film.

clue.text: Panel team designed as sign of ownership

indicators.note: designed suggests the letters are put together in a new form

explanation.surface: A panel of experts devises a badge of ownership.
explanation.walkthrough: 'designed' rearranges the letters of PANEL TEAM.
explanation.definitionFit: A nameplate on a door or object shows who it belongs to, a sign of ownership.

clue.text: Time in history needed to muse

parts.note: an era is a period of time in history

explanation.surface: Someone needs time to ponder the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'muse' looks like a verb meaning ponder, but it is the noun: one of the nine Muses.
explanation.definitionFit: Erato is one of the nine Muses of Greek myth, presiding over lyric and love poetry.

clue.text: Having thieved around estate, I'm with police at last — so cheap

indicators.note: around means the first piece wraps the second

parts.note: nicked is British slang for stolen
an estate is land

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter of police

explanation.surface: A thief who has robbed an estate meets the police, and comes off cheaply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' is the container signal and 'at last' takes the final letter of police; nickel and dime are small US coins.
explanation.definitionFit: Nickel-and-dime, from small US coins, describes something petty or cheap.
